name: LightningXML
workload: Deserializes matching-struct XML payloads across 9 synthetic shapes (flat, deep, attributes, small, large 10K-user, org/nested, tree depth-14, comment-heavy, catalog) into typed C++ records; measures source-bytes-per-second throughput, pinned to one core, median of 15 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: Leads every workload: e.g. Flat 3.82 GB/s vs pugixml 1.46 GB/s, RapidXML 199 MB/s, libxml2 DOM 178 MB/s; Large(10K users) 3.31 GB/s vs pugixml 311 MB/s, libxml2 DOM 60 MB/s; Attributes 1.91 GB/s vs libxml2 DOM 34 MB/s; Comment-heavy 13.22 GB/s vs pugixml 2.87 GB/s
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, Ubuntu 24.04, pinned to one core
tradeoffs: Zero-copy/non-normalizing default parser trades entity decoding and validation for speed; requires compile-time field-mapping structs rather than a general DOM API; StrictParser tier restores well-formedness checks at reduced speed; C++20 required.
caveats: Single-project, first-party benchmark (not independent); author flags the depth-14 Tree row as allocation-bound/high-variance for the DOM competitors (pugixml/RapidXML); very new/low-adoption project (1 star, created June 2026).

name: yam
workload: Parses generated YAML/JSON shapes (block mappings/sequences, mixed block+flow+quoted, JSON, config files with comments/anchors) plus real files repeated to ~10MB (travis.yml, appveyor.yml, compile_commands.json) and scalar-heavy block-scalar text, via `make bench-compare`.
claimed_speedup: 1.6-13x faster than libyaml 0.2.5 and libfyaml 0.9.6 across inputs: e.g. config files 206 MB/s vs libyaml 125 MB/s; travis.yml 501 MB/s vs libyaml 149 MB/s; literal block scalars 3091 MB/s vs libyaml 290 MB/s
tradeoffs: C11 event/token-stream API rather than a DOM by default (a separate document layer would need to be built on top); zero-copy string spans require the source buffer to stay alive for the parser's lifetime; brand-new project competing with long-established libyaml/libfyaml.
caveats: First-party benchmark run on the author's own single machine/single core via `make bench-compare`; not yet independently reproduced; 0 stars and active only since Feb 2026.

name: chyaml
workload: Parses/materializes a 4.63MB synthetic YAML file (50,000 records, 15 alternating paired runs) plus an 8-shape workload matrix (mixed records, flat mapping, scalar sequence, nested mappings, flow sequences, quoted strings, sparse values/comments, long scalars) comparing chyaml's fast event tape against rapidyaml 0.16.0's arena tree.
claimed_speedup: ~2.13x faster than rapidyaml on the primary workload (391 MB/s vs 184 MB/s) with ~13.18x less incremental memory; across the 8-shape matrix, 1.16x-2.16x faster per shape (aggregate 1.92x, geometric mean 1.90x), memory 1.63x-14.55x less
tradeoffs: Reported speedups target chyaml's portable 8-byte fast-path event tape, which only covers common configuration-YAML shapes; input outside that subset falls back to a slower 'complete path' for full YAML 1.2.2 grammar (directives, complex keys, full block-scalar handling), where a separate matrix shows only 1.03x-7.22x; comparison executables link rapidyaml only for benchmarking, never into the shipped library.
caveats: First-party, self-run benchmark, not independently reproduced; baseline used is rapidyaml (a well-known fast YAML library already on the catalogued KNOWN_LIST) rather than one of this run's five named baselines, so baseline_in_list=false; author explicitly calls out nested-mappings as the weakest case (1.16x).

name: frxml
workload: Parses synthetic XML files from roughly 10 KiB to 330 KiB, benchmarked with a google/benchmark harness (bundled as a git submodule) against pugixml, tinyxml2, RapidXML, and libxml2.
claimed_speedup: frxml fastest across the whole size range: pugixml and RapidXML run at ~0.6-1.0x of frxml's parse time (frxml ~1.0-1.7x faster), libxml2 runs ~2-5.8x slower than frxml, tinyxml2 ~4-5x slower than frxml (from docs/Figure_1.png log-scale relative-elapsed chart); frxml also shows the lowest allocated memory throughout
tradeoffs: Zero-copy/single-pass design explicitly omits entity and DOCTYPE/ENTITY decoding to stay zero-copy, and only supports a limited XML 1.0 subset; goal of O(n) memory regardless of nesting depth.
caveats: Numbers exist only as a chart image (Figure_1.png), not as text/table, with no compiler flags or CPU model stated anywhere in the repo; it is the project's own benchmark harness, so capped at tier C rather than B; the GitHub repository is archived (author has abandoned it).

name: TupleMarkup (TML)
workload: Parsing unspecified sample data with the bundled C89 in-place TML parser (tml-c), informally compared to libxml2 parsing 'the same data'.
claimed_speedup: "about 5x faster than Libxml2 when parsing the same data", with dramatically less memory use (per tml-c/README; no numeric table or workload description given)
tradeoffs: TML is a distinct minimalist markup language (bracket-minimized nested lists) rather than XML itself, so adopting it means replacing XML documents wholesale, not a drop-in libxml2 substitute; in-place parsing needs no malloc and targets no-heap embedded use; C89-compatible.
caveats: No benchmark methodology, workload size, compiler, or hardware stated anywhere -- a bare first-party numeric claim; project untouched since 2013 (abandoned); the comparison is between a custom markup format's parser and an XML parser, so treat the 'faster than libxml2' claim as weak/indirect evidence.
